title: The Belonging Belief
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: The capstone belief in Stuart's Five Key Beliefs pyramid, Belonging asks two intertwined questions in a student's heart: who am I, and does who I am fit here. Stuart explains why Belonging signals are inherently ambiguous, and how, left untreated, ambiguous interpretation becomes recursive, spiraling into what he calls the anti-Belonging doom loop of demotivation, self-sabotage, procrastination, and isolation. He grounds the discussion in research on imposter syndrome and stereotype threat, and highlights the Values Affirmation intervention, a simple writing exercise shown in multiple studies to cut suspension and office-referral gaps and raise grades among stereotype-threatened students.
points: Stuart's central mechanism is the ambiguity of social signals, and Belonging is the lens students use to interpret those signals as safe or threatening.
The anti-Belonging doom loop traces how an entrenched belief compounds itself, culminating in a moment of attribution where both success and failure get read as proof of not belonging.
He distinguishes imposter syndrome, the feeling of being a fraud, from stereotype threat, fear of confirming a negative group stereotype, citing the founding research for each.

A study of 2,000 middle schoolers across 11 racially diverse schools found that a twice-yearly Values Affirmation writing exercise cut the Black-white suspension and office-referral gap by two-thirds.
quotes: Who am I? What is my identity? What makes me, me? Does who I am fit here — with these people, studying this discipline, doing this kind of work?
This is the trouble with signals in social contexts: They are ambiguous. They require interpretation.

Because our student has a heavily entrenched anti-Belonging belief — and because of the ambiguity of Belonging signals — he is likely to interpret either success or failure in the same way — proof that he doesn't belong.

Imposter syndrome, first named by Clance and Imes in 1978, is the feeling students have when they are convinced they don't belong and are in fact acting fraudulently when engaging in a given academic pursuit.
Stereotype threat is related but different. This phenomena happens when a student is concerned about confirming negative stereotypes that may be held about their group.
In the months after the intervention, The black-white suspension and office referral gaps were cut by two-thirds, with an even more positive impact on black students with prior infractions.
As with all interventions like this, it is far from a silver bullet. But given the simplicity of the task and the wonderful things you can learn about your students, it's a total no-brainer.
